title: Three Things Held Dear

zh.text: 天下皆謂我道大，似不肖。夫唯大，故似不肖。若肖，久矣其細也夫！

gloss.4: I, my (the speaker; no sage is named in this passage)
gloss.10: xiào: to resemble, as a child resembles a parent; 不肖: unlike; also “unworthy”

zh.text: 我有三寶，持而保之。一曰慈，二曰儉，三曰不敢為天下先。

gloss.7: bǎo: to guard, to keep safe (the same sound as 寶)
gloss.12: cí: a parent’s tender love for a child
gloss.16: jiǎn: sparing; to hold in, to use little

zh.text: 不敢為天下先，故能成器長。

gloss.10: vessel; a made thing; a person of ability, an official

gloss.1: shě: to let go, to throw away (later written 捨)
gloss.3: and yet go for; Wang Bi: “to take”

zh.text: 舍儉且廣，舍後且先，死矣！
以守則固。天將救之，以慈衛之。

gloss.7: to rescue, to save from danger
gloss.12: to guard, to stand guard around

rendering: All under heaven say that [[my Dao|wodao]] is great
and seems to [[take after nothing|buxiao]].
Because it is great, it seems to take after nothing.
If it took after something,
how long it would have been [[small|xi]]!
I have [[three things to treasure|sanbao]].
I hold them and [[keep them safe|bao]].
The first is [[tenderness|ci]].
The second is [[spareness|jian]].
The third is [[not daring to go ahead of the world|xian]].
Tender, and so able to be [[brave|yong]].
Sparing, and so able to be wide.
Not daring to go ahead of the world,
and so able to be [[head of the finished vessels|qizhang]].
Now: to let go of tenderness and [[take|qie]] courage,
to let go of spareness and take width,
to let go of [[the rear and take the front|hou-xian-pair]]:
[[that is death|si]].
Tenderness: [[fight with it and win|zhan]];
defend with it and stand firm.
Whom heaven will [[rescue|jiu]],
it [[guards with tenderness|wei]].

wodao.title: 我道: who says “I”?
wodao.body: Most of the Laozi has no speaker. Here, and in passages 20 and 70, a voice says 我, “I”. We keep 道 as Dao: it is a road, a way of doing, and the way all things go, and no English word holds the three. The received text has 我道大, “my Dao is great”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to have no 道: 天下皆謂我大，不肖, “all under heaven say that I am great, and unlike”. That older line is odder and more personal. The world’s complaint is about the speaker: too large, and of no use, like nothing that people know. “My Dao” makes it a remark about a teaching, and Legge goes further and adds “(to other systems of teaching)”. Who is the “I”? An old teacher, the sage as a type, or the Dao itself. The text does not say. Read it once in each voice.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B (as reported)

buxiao.title: 不肖: the child who is unlike
buxiao.body: 肖 is “to resemble”, and it is a family word. The Shuowen: 骨肉相似也, “bone and flesh are alike”, and then 不似其先，故曰“不肖”也: “one who is not like his forebears is therefore called 不肖”. In everyday classical Chinese 不肖 means “unworthy, good for nothing”: a son who does not take after the father. So the world’s remark has an edge that English loses. They say: your Dao is great, and it is a worthless child that resembles no one. The speaker takes the insult and agrees. It is unlike because it is great. Passage 4 has already said of the Dao: 吾不知誰之子, “I do not know whose child it is”. There is one more turn. The sound part of 肖 is 小, “small”. To resemble is, in the character itself, to be small.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 肉部: 肖，骨肉相似也。从肉小聲。不似其先，故曰“不肖”也。

xi.title: Wang Bi: what can be compared is small
xi.body: 久矣其細也夫 is an exclamation with the order turned round, and Wang Bi first puts it straight: 久矣其細，猶曰其細久矣, “‘long indeed, its smallness’ is the same as ‘its smallness would be of long standing’”. Then he gives the reason in one line: 肖，則失其所以為大矣. “If it resembled, it would lose that by which it is great.” 細 is “fine, thin”; the character has silk thread, 糸, at the left. A thing that is like another thing can be set beside it, measured, ranked, and given a use. That is what it means to be small. The same test works on a person. The parts of you that can be compared are the parts that can be ranked. What in you is like nothing?

sanbao.title: 三寶 before the Buddhists
sanbao.body: Today 三寶 is known across East Asia as a Buddhist term: the Three Jewels, which are the Buddha, the teaching, and the community. That use is later. When Buddhist texts were put into Chinese, from the 2nd century CE on, translators used this phrase, which Chinese readers knew from the Laozi. Daoist religion later answered with its own three: the Dao, the scriptures, the masters. In the Warring States period the phrase meant something else again. Mencius says: 諸侯之寶三：土地、人民、政事, “the treasures of a lord are three: land, people, and government”. That is a list of what a state owns. Against it, this passage’s three are strange. Not one of them is a possession. All three are ways of holding back. A ruler who heard 我有三寶 expected jade.

bao.title: 寶 and 保: treasure and keep
bao.body: 我有三寶，持而保之. The noun 寶, “treasure”, and the verb 保, “to keep safe”, are the same sound, bǎo, and the Chinese ear hears: “three bǎo; I hold them and bǎo them”. A treasure is that which is kept. The character 寶 is a small storehouse. The Shuowen lists its parts: 从宀从王从貝，缶聲, a roof 宀, jade (written 王 here), a cowrie shell 貝, which was early money, and 缶, a jar, for the sound. Jade and shells under a roof: what a household guards. 保, in the Shuowen, is 養也, “to nurture”, and its early form is commonly explained as a person with a child on the back. So even the verb for guarding these treasures is a word of child care. The treasures return in passage 69: 輕敵幾喪吾寶.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 宀部: 寶，珍也。从宀从王从貝，缶聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 人部: 保，養也。

ci.title: 慈: love that goes downward
ci.body: 慈 has no good English word. It is the love of a parent for a child, and above all of a mother: 慈母 is the set phrase. It runs downward, from the stronger to the weaker, and its partner is 孝, the child’s devotion, which runs upward (passages 18 and 19 name the pair). “Compassion” is the usual choice, but that word came to 慈 later, when Buddhists used it to translate their term for kindness to all beings. “Mercy” assumes a judge who could punish. [[Legge’s|legge]] “gentleness” is a manner. 慈 is none of these. It is fierce: it feeds, carries, and stands in front. The book calls the Dao the mother of the world (25, 52). The first treasure is to hold things as that mother does. We write “tenderness” and ask you to hear the mother in it.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 心部: 慈，愛也。从心兹聲。

jian.title: 儉: not “economy”
jian.body: 儉 is to use little and hold much in. The Shuowen says 約也, and 約 is “to wind round and tie”: a bundle bound tight. Legge writes “economy”, a word of Victorian household accounts. “Moderation” brings Aristotle’s mean between two extremes. “Frugality” is nearer, but it sounds like saving money. 儉 is wider: few words, few wants, few orders, little display. Confucius used the word of ritual: better sparing than lavish. Wang Bi explains the result: 節儉愛費，天下不匱，故能廣也, “sparing and careful of cost, so that the world does not run short; and so one can be wide”. This is the logic of a reservoir. That which is not spent is there when it is needed. Passage 59 praises a different word, 嗇, the farmer’s care in storing grain. What do you spend that you do not notice?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 人部: 儉，約也。从人僉聲。

xian.title: A treasure made of “not”
xian.body: The first two treasures have one character each. The third needs six: 不敢為天下先, “not daring to act as the front of all under heaven”. Chinese had words for modesty and for yielding, and the text does not use them. It describes a refusal. And 不敢, “not dare”, is the phrase of a junior before a senior; it names a real fear, the kind that one has on thin ice. It is not a quiet opinion about one’s rank. The line does not say “be last”. It says: do not make yourself the first. The front is a place that others may [[push one into|qizhang]]; see passage 66. In modern China the phrase lost its negative and became a slogan of reform: 敢為天下先, “dare to be the first under heaven”. Two characters fewer, and a treasure thrown away. Which do you hear more often?

yong.title: 勇: courage with a root
yong.body: 慈故能勇: “tender, and so able to be brave”. The small word 故, “and so”, makes a claim about cause. Courage is not a first thing. It grows from care, as a hen’s attack on a hawk grows from the chicks. The Shuowen defines 勇 in one word: 气也, “it is breath”, the surge of energy in the body. The lower part of the character is 力, strength. Courage alone is only that surge. Confucius made the same cut: the humane are sure to have courage, and the brave are not sure to be humane. Passage 73 divides courage in two by its direction: courage in daring kills, and courage in not-daring keeps alive. English “brave” is praise with no conditions. Here the question is always: brave from what?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 力部: 勇，气也。从力甬聲。

qizhang.title: 成器長: chief of the vessels
qizhang.body: 器 is a vessel, then any finished tool, then a person shaped for one use: an official. Passage 28 gives the picture: when the uncarved wood is split, it becomes vessels, and the sage, using them, becomes 官長, head of the officials. So 成器長 is “head of the finished vessels”: the one who can lead all those who have a function, and who has no fixed function. Legge turns the phrase round and makes the sage himself “a vessel of the highest honour”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 故能為成事長, “and so can be head of the completed affairs”, and Han Fei quotes the line in that form. In both, the logic is that of passage 66. The one who does not take the front is the one whom others will have at the front.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B (as reported)

qie.title: 舍 … 且: a small word that English must fix
qie.body: 今舍慈且勇: “now, let go of tenderness, 且 courage”. 舍 is 捨, “to throw away”. 且 is a small word with several jobs: “moreover”, “for the moment”, “and yet”. Wang Bi gives it a rare gloss: 且，猶取也, “且 is like 取, to take”. On his reading the line has two verbs, drop and take. Others keep the common sense: “let go of tenderness and yet be brave”. The meaning is close in both. People want the fruit and cut the root. The word 今, “now, these days”, makes it a complaint about the speaker’s own age. No subject is named. It can be the rulers of the time, or anyone. We follow Wang Bi and write “take”, because it shows the hand that grabs.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 67: 且，猶取也。

si.title: 死矣: three ambitions of the age
si.body: 死矣 is two syllables: “dead”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to be longer and no softer: 則必死矣, “then death is certain”. Look at what was grabbed. 勇, courage, was the prized quality of the Warring States: Qin gave ranks of nobility for enemy heads, and lords kept swordsmen who died to show their daring. 廣, width, was state policy; to “widen the land” by taking a neighbour’s territory was the normal aim of a court. 先, to be first, was the dream of each king: to be hegemon and then sole ruler. The passage names the three ambitions of its time and calls each one a fruit cut from its root. It was written while those states were destroying one another. Within about a century of the oldest copies, every one of them was gone.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B (as reported)

zhan.title: Wang Bi: why the tender win
zhan.body: A line about love now speaks of battle, and this troubles readers who want the book to be gentle. The claim is practical. Wang Bi: 相慜而不避於難，故勝也, “they feel for one another and do not turn away from hardship; so they win”. An army whose members care for each other does not break. The strategists said the same from the commander’s side. The Sunzi says: look on your soldiers as infants, and they will go with you into deep ravines; look on them as beloved sons, and they will die beside you. Note the second half of the Laozi line: 以守則固, “defend with it and stand firm”. The stress is on holding. A mother is the picture: she does not look for a fight, and nothing moves her from the door.

jiu.title: 救 or 建: rescue, or set up
jiu.body: The received text says 天將救之，以慈衛之: “heaven will rescue them; with tenderness it guards them”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 天將建之，如以茲垣之: “heaven will set them up; it is as if it walled them round with 茲”. Two things differ. 建 is “to establish, to set upright”, the word of passage 54, where that which is well established is not pulled up. And the verb for guarding is 垣, a wall of earth; the Shuowen says 牆也, “a wall”. Their 茲 is our [[慈|ci]], written with no heart beneath it. In both versions heaven is not a god with a will. 天 is the sky and the order of things. The line can also be read the other way: the one whom heaven means to save is the one to whom it gives tenderness.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B (as reported)
Shuowen Jiezi, 土部: 垣，牆也。从土亘聲。

wei.title: 衛: guards who walk in a ring
wei.body: 衛 is a military word. The Shuowen, which writes it 衞, says 宿衞也, “the night guard”, and explains the outer part: 行，列衞也, “行 is the ranks of the guards”. Look at the character: the two halves of 行, a crossroads, stand at left and right, and the middle part is commonly explained as feet that go round a walled place. It is a picture of a patrol. The word named the troops around a ruler and a state in the central plain. So the last line is exact: tenderness is posted around a person like sentries at night. English “protect” is general. 衛 is a ring of living guards, and it is used here of the least warlike thing in the book. Who stands guard around you, and around whom do you stand?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 行部: 衞，宿衞也。从韋、帀，从行。行，列衞也。

legge.title: Legge: gentleness, economy, shrinking
legge.body: Legge’s three are “gentleness”, “economy”, and “shrinking from taking precedence of others”. Each is a virtue of a Victorian Christian household: a mild manner, careful accounts, and good behaviour at a door. They are not wrong, and they are small. [[慈|ci]] becomes a temperament where the Chinese has a mother’s force; [[儉|jian]] becomes thrift; and the third becomes etiquette, with “shrinking” for [[不敢|xian]]. He then reads 成器長 as “a vessel of the highest honour”, which echoes “a vessel unto honour” in the letters of Paul, and so brings the sage near the New Testament. His first paragraph adds “systems of teaching” twice in brackets. A missionary and scholar of religions saw rival doctrines there. The Chinese says only that the speaker is like nothing.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

practice.title: Find the root of one brave act
practice.body: Take the three pairs as three checks, one for each part of a day. Morning, courage: you will have to do one hard thing today, such as a refusal, a hard talk, or a risk. Before it, ask what it protects. If you can name a person or a living thing that you care for, go on; the courage has its root. If you find only the wish to look strong, wait. Midday, width: before you take on one more thing, look for one thing to use less of. Evening, the front: recall a moment when you made yourself first, in a queue, in a talk, in credit for work. Do not blame yourself. Notice what it cost, and who felt it. The passage says of the three: [[持而保之|bao]]. They are kept by daily handling.

hou-xian-pair.title: 後 and 先, 慈 and 勇: root and fruit
hou-xian-pair.body: The passage gives three pairs: tenderness and courage (慈, 勇), spareness and width (儉, 廣), the rear and the front (後, 先). They look like opposites, and a quick reader ranks them: tender good, brave bad. The text says a different thing. Each first term produces the second: tender, 故, [[and so able to be brave|yong]]. Courage, width, and the head’s place are wanted, and they are reached. What the text calls death is to [[take|qie]] the second with the first let go: the fruit cut from the root. So the preference is for an order, and not for one side. It answers an age that grabbed at the front. The favoured side also turns. Tenderness goes out to fight in the last lines, and the one who stays behind becomes [[head|qizhang]]. What of tenderness from which no courage grows? The text does not name it. But it is the root that bears which is treasured here.

lenses.ground: The passage opens with a complaint and an answer. The world says the speaker’s [[Dao|wodao]] is great and [[takes after nothing|buxiao]]. Yes, says the speaker: anything that took after something would long since have been [[small|xi]]. Then comes the centre: [[three precious things|sanbao]], held and [[kept|bao]]: [[tenderness|ci]], [[spareness|jian]], and a [[refusal to go first|xian]]. Each one produces its seeming opposite: tenderness gives courage, spareness gives width, the rear place gives [[the head’s place|qizhang]]. Then a warning in the same three steps: take the fruit with no root, and [[you are dead|si]]. The end returns to the first treasure alone and sets it in a war: it wins, it holds, and [[heaven posts it around|wei]] those it would save.
lenses.inner: The three precious things are not rules. Each is a way that attention can hold what comes before it. [[慈|ci]] is to meet one’s own states as a mother meets a child: the fear, the dull morning, the failure are all hers, and she turns none of them out. [[儉|jian]] is to spend little: fewer comments on experience, fewer plans laid over the present hour. The third is to let each moment arrive before the mind [[runs in front of it|xian]] to say what it is. Then the opening lines read differently. A self that is like something, that can be described and ranked, is [[small|xi]]. What you are when you are compared with nothing has no size. The speaker holds that with open hands, and so it is called a treasure.
lenses.leading: Every organization praises the right-hand column: courage, reach, leadership. This passage says that each one is an effect, and it names the causes. Bold decisions that hold come from care for the people who will bear them. Reach comes from restraint, as a firm that spends little can go far. And the front place is safe only for the one who [[did not seize it|xian]]. The warning is the most practical line in the passage. A leader who lets go of the left-hand column and keeps the right is reckless, overextended, and self-promoting, and the text says that this ends in [[death|si]]: of the venture, or the state, or the person. The age that produced these lines proved it. The question for a team is always the same: brave [[from what|yong]]?
lenses.body: In a body the three precious things can be felt. [[Tenderness|ci]] is a soft chest and belly: the front of the body does not armour itself, and for that reason the back and legs can be strong. Fighters know that a tight, angry body is slow; the one who protects something is quick and does not tire. [[Spareness|jian]] is economy of movement: no extra tension, no wasted step, the breath kept low. A master of any art looks as if little is done. [[Not going first|xian]] is timing: let the other move, and answer. The final lines give the martial result in two verbs: [[win and hold|zhan]]. Stand for a moment as if a small child were asleep behind you. Feel what that does to the feet.
lenses.practice: Do the three checks of [[the practice note|practice]]: a root for one brave act, one thing to use less of, one moment at the front to recall. Then take the opening lines as a short meditation. Sit, and finish the sentence “I am like…” five times, with whatever comes: like my father, like other people of my trade, like a tired person. Each answer is true and each is [[small|xi]]. Then stop the sentence at “I am” and sit for one minute with no comparison. The world may call that [[good for nothing|buxiao]]. The speaker of this passage calls it great.

plates.title: The loving stone
plates.lesson: At the foot is 心, the heart. Above it is 兹. The Shuowen gives 慈 as 愛也, “to love”, with 兹 as the sound, and it enters that sound part as 玆: 黑也。从二玄, “black; from two 玄”, two dark twists of thread, the shape 幺 that is also in 絲, silk. A separate entry, 茲, with grass on top, is 艸木多益, “plants and trees that grow more and more”; the two characters merged in use. The same sound part is in 滋, to moisten, to nourish, and 孳, to breed, to bear young. So the family of 慈 is about increase and feeding, though the dictionary claims only the sound. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word in this passage with no heart, as plain 茲. The best cousin is a surprise. The modern word for a magnet is 磁石. Early texts write it 慈石, “the loving stone”. The Lüshi chunqiu, about 240 BCE, says 慈石召鐵, “the loving stone calls iron”, and a Han commentator explains that the stone is the mother of iron and draws her child to her. A stone radical was put under it later to make 磁. This is the force that the [[first treasure|ci]] names. It does not push or command. It draws, and what it draws comes home. Our word “magnet” is only a Greek place name.
plates.brush: Thirteen strokes. First a dot, then a short stroke that falls to the left: two small tips. Third a long horizontal, which is the roof of the character. Under it come the two threads, left then right. Each thread is three strokes: a stroke that goes down to the left and turns back to the right; a second, larger one of the same kind; and a dot. Watch the two threads: they are twins, and the right one is written a little larger and slightly higher. Last comes the heart: a dot at the left, a long hook that lies almost flat and flicks up at its end, a dot inside the curve, and a dot at the right. The heart is the base, and it should be as wide as the roof. In clerical script the threads are small and round, and the heart spreads like a boat.

plates.title: Many mouths, one voice
plates.lesson: The left side is 亻, a standing person, the form that 人 takes at the side of a character. It tells you that the word is about human conduct. The right side is 僉. The Shuowen says of 僉: 皆也。从亼从吅从从, “all, together. From 亼 (to gather), 吅 (two mouths), and 从 (two people)”. Read it from the top: a roof-like sign of gathering, two mouths, two persons. Several people speak as one: “all”. In 儉 this part gives the sound, and it gives the sound to a large family: 檢, to inspect (the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to use this character for the [[second treasure|jian]]); 驗, to verify; 險, a narrow, dangerous pass; 劍, a sword; 臉, the face; and 斂, to gather in, to draw tight. Scholars often note that 儉 and 斂 are close in sense as well as sound: both are a drawing-in. The Shuowen defines 儉 as 約也, “to bind”. So one can read the character as a person who gathers many things into one and ties them. The opposite word is 奢, “lavish”, which the Shuowen explains as 張也, “to stretch open”. One closes and one opens. Confucius set the two side by side: in ritual, rather 儉 than 奢. The short form 俭 keeps the person and reduces the crowd to three small strokes.
plates.brush: Fifteen strokes. The person first: a stroke that falls to the left, then a vertical beneath it. Then the right side, from the top. A long stroke falls to the left and a long stroke falls to the right; they meet at the peak and make the roof. A short horizontal sits under the peak. Then the left mouth: left side; top and right side with one corner; base. Then the right mouth, with the same three strokes in the same order. Then the left small person: a stroke to the left, and a dot. Then the right small person: a stroke to the left, and a last stroke to the right. Watch the roof. Its two strokes must reach wide enough to cover all that stands under them, the mouths and the persons. The lesson of the form is the lesson of the word: eleven small strokes are held in order by two.

plates.title: A foot ahead of a person
plates.lesson: The Shuowen says: 前進也。从儿从之, “to go forward. From 儿 (a person) and 之 (to go)”. The lower two strokes, 儿, are a person’s legs. The upper part was 之, and in the oldest forms 之 is commonly explained as a foot on a line: a foot that sets out. So the early character is a foot drawn above a person: someone whose foot has already gone, the one in front. From “ahead in space” came “ahead in time”: 先 is “earlier, former”. 先生, “born before”, is a teacher, and today the plain word for “Mr.”. 先王 are the former kings. And 先 alone means forebears, the dead of the family: the Shuowen’s own entry on [[不肖|buxiao]] speaks of the child who is not like 其先. This gives the third treasure a second edge. 不敢為天下先 is not to dare to be the world’s forerunner, and also not to set oneself up as the world’s ancestor, the one from whom all must descend. The opposite word is 後, “behind, after”. The Shuowen defines it 遲也, “late”, and lists its parts: 彳, a step; 幺, a thread; 夊, a foot that drags. A foot on a thread walks behind. In this passage the foot that goes ahead is the [[dangerous one|xian]], and the foot that comes after is safe.
plates.brush: Six strokes. First a short stroke that falls to the left. Second a horizontal that starts from it. Third a vertical through that horizontal, from above it to below. Fourth a long horizontal: the ground line, and the widest stroke of the upper part. Then the legs. The fifth stroke falls to the left in a long curve. The sixth goes down, bends to the right, runs along the base, and ends in a hook that turns up. Watch the sixth stroke. It is the largest movement in the character, and it carries the weight like a foot set well forward. The upper part should be small and upright, and the legs wide. In running script the last stroke is often left open, with no hook, and the brush leaves the paper on its way to the next character.

questions.claim: Courage that lasts grows out of tenderness; courage taken with no such root ends in death.
prompts: Think of the bravest thing that you have done. What was it for? Was care under it, or something else?
Were you taught that tenderness and courage go together, or that one must be given up for the other? By whom?
Hold the opposite: tenderness makes a person hesitate, and the brave act needs a hard heart. When have you believed that?
Which do you show more readily, the tender side or the brave one? What do you fear would happen if the other were seen?

questions.claim: The one who does not dare to go ahead of the world can become its head.
prompts: Do you agree? Where have you seen a person reach the front because they did not seize it?
What is your own relation to being first: do you want it, avoid it, or deny that you want it?
Put the modern slogan in its place: dare to be first. Stay with it. What does it wake up in you?
If you hold back, is it this treasure, or is it fear in the treasure’s clothes? How would you know?

questions.claim: Spending little is what makes it possible to reach far.
prompts: Is this true in your use of money, words, or strength? Where has it failed?
What did your family teach about spending and saving? Did that come from want, from fear, or from choice?
Hold the other side: what is spent freely comes back, and a tight hand makes a small life. Which side resists in you?
What do you judge in people who spend in the way that you do not?
